overview: News Corporation is a global media and information services company operating through five segments: Dow Jones (Wall Street Journal, Barron's, MarketWatch, Factiva, Dow Jones Risk & Compliance), Digital Real Estate Services (majority stake in REA Group, majority stake in Move Inc./realtor.com), Book Publishing (HarperCollins), News Media (New York Post, The Sun, The Times/Sunday Times, Australian mastheads, news.com.au, talkSPORT), and Other. The company completed the sale of its Foxtel pay-TV business to DAZN in April 2025, sharpening its focus on digital subscription and real estate growth engines. Fiscal year ends June 30; the company is controlled by the Murdoch family via a dual-class share structure (NWS non-voting Class B / NWSA voting Class A).

business_model.summary: A diversified portfolio shifting from print/advertising toward digital subscriptions, data/analytics licensing, and digital real estate marketplaces. Over 60% of revenue is now digital, with Dow Jones and REA Group (Digital Real Estate) the primary profit engines, supplemented by HarperCollins' project-based book publishing and News Media's advertising/subscription mix. Emerging AI content-licensing deals (OpenAI, Meta, Bloomberg) are a new high-margin revenue stream monetizing News Corp's content archives.

revenue_streams.name: Dow Jones (WSJ, Barron's, Factiva, Risk & Compliance)
Digital Real Estate Services (REA Group, Move/realtor.com)
News Media (NY Post, The Sun, The Times, Australian mastheads)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (digital subscriptions to WSJ, news mastheads, book buyers) and B2B (Dow Jones Risk & Compliance data/analytics, real estate agent/advertiser listings, AI licensing to tech companies)
business_model.geographic_mix: United States ~60%, Australia ~20%, United Kingdom ~12%, Rest of World ~8% (approximate, varies by segment)

competitive_position.market_position: Leading global business/financial news franchise (WSJ, Dow Jones) and dominant digital real estate marketplace in Australia (REA Group #1); challenger position in US real estate (realtor.com #3 behind Zillow); top-5 global trade book publisher

moat_factors.description: WSJ, The Times and other mastheads carry decades of brand authority that commands premium subscription pricing and advertiser trust
REA Group's dominant Australian listings platform benefits from two-sided network effects between agents and buyers, driving pricing power
Decades of archived journalism and data are now a unique licensable asset for AI model training (OpenAI, Meta deals)

moat_factors.factor: Scale in data/analytics (Dow Jones Risk & Compliance)
moat_factors.description: Factiva/Risk & Compliance embedded in enterprise compliance workflows creates switching costs
HarperCollins' backlist catalog provides durable, low-capex royalty income

weaknesses: News Media segment structurally declining as print advertising and circulation erode
Partial (not wholly-owned) stakes in key digital real estate assets (REA Group, Move Inc.) mean non-controlling interests absorb a share of segment profit
Dual-class share structure concentrates control with the Murdoch family, limiting influence of outside shareholders and creating governance/succession risk
Heavy reliance on just two segments (Dow Jones, Digital Real Estate) for the bulk of profitability

growth_drivers: Dow Jones digital subscription growth and enterprise Risk & Compliance/data products, with a stated target of $1 billion in Dow Jones EBITDA within five years
REA Group yield growth, listings volume recovery, and expansion into adjacent property services (mortgage broking, data)
AI content-licensing deals (OpenAI >$250M, Meta ~$50M/year, expanded Bloomberg deal) monetizing archival content with minimal incremental cost
Continued margin expansion post-Foxtel divestiture, simplifying the portfolio around higher-margin digital pillars
HarperCollins backlist and strong front-list performance supporting stable profitability
Potential further capital return (buybacks) given improved balance sheet following Foxtel sale proceeds

business.risk: Secular decline in print advertising and circulation
business.description: News Media segment revenue continues to erode structurally, pressuring overall growth even as digital segments grow
REA Group and Move/realtor.com revenues are tied to property listing volumes and transaction activity, sensitive to mortgage rates and housing market health
AI Overviews and chatbots reduce referral traffic to publisher sites even as News Corp also monetizes AI licensing deals; a long-term threat to subscription and advertising funnels

business.risk: Competitive pressure in real estate from Zillow/CoStar
business.description: realtor.com (Move Inc.) trails Zillow in US market share and faces renewed competitive intensity

financial.description: Significant AUD and GBP revenue exposure (REA Group, UK News Media) creates translation volatility versus USD reporting
REA Group and other partly-owned subsidiaries mean a portion of segment EBITDA accrues to minority holders

regulatory.description: News Corp and peer publishers are entangled in Google ad-tech MDL litigation and DOJ monopoly remedy proceedings; Google has subpoenaed News Corp for AI licensing records, creating legal and reputational exposure

regulatory.risk: News bargaining/media regulation in Australia and UK
regulatory.description: Ongoing regulatory efforts (e.g., Australian News Bargaining Incentive, UK press regulation) could affect commercial terms with tech platforms
Dow Jones Risk & Compliance and real estate data businesses face evolving global privacy rules

macro.risk: Interest rate sensitivity of housing markets
macro.description: Management flagged higher mortgage rates as a potential headwind to real estate listing/transaction volumes in FY2027
News Media and some Dow Jones advertising revenue remain exposed to broader economic/ad-spend cycles

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Traditional print media in secular decline; digital subscriptions, B2B data/analytics, and digital real estate marketplaces are structurally growing; AI licensing is an emerging, fast-growing revenue category for content owners
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - advertising and real estate transaction volumes are cyclical; subscription and data/analytics revenue (Dow Jones, Risk & Compliance) is more resilient/recurring
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate, primarily via housing transaction volumes affecting Digital Real Estate Services (REA Group, Move)
key_input_costs: Paper and raw materials for book publishing

recent_developments.event: Completed sale of Foxtel Group to DAZN; News Corp received ~6% equity stake in DAZN plus repayment of ~A$592M in shareholder loans, simplifying the portfolio around core growth pillars

Reported Q4 and full-year FY2026 results: FY2026 revenue $9.03B (+7%), Total Segment EBITDA $1.63B (+15%), margin expanded from 16.7% to 18%; Q4 net income from continuing operations up 167% YoY to $230M
Management set a target for Dow Jones to reach $1 billion in EBITDA within five years and highlighted record profitability driven by AI partnerships and digital growth
Expanded AI content-licensing partnerships including deals with OpenAI (reportedly valued at over $250M) and Meta (~$50M/year), plus an expanded Bloomberg deal for Dow Jones AI content rights

Google subpoenaed News Corp for records on its AI/search licensing deals as part of DOJ monopoly-remedy litigation; separately, a federal judge dismissed multiple publishers' antitrust claims against Google over AI Overviews (Sept 30, 2026), while Google ad-tech MDL litigation involving other publishers proceeds toward trial
Digital Real Estate Services revenue rose 17% to $473M including 20% growth at REA Group; Dow Jones revenue up 8% to $619M with Risk & Compliance up 16%

items.notes: Management expects continued revenue growth across core growth pillars (Dow Jones, Digital Real Estate, Book Publishing)

items.target: further EBITDA margin expansion from FY2026's 18%
items.notes: Company described itself as encouraged by the prospect of further margin expansion in the current fiscal year
Long-term target introduced on FY2026 earnings call, up from FY2026 Dow Jones EBITDA of $663 million
Caveat that higher mortgage rates may weigh on real estate transaction activity

guidance.management_commentary: Management emphasized record full-year profitability, the strategic benefit of simplifying the portfolio after the Foxtel divestiture, and the emerging contribution from AI content-licensing deals as a new high-margin revenue stream. The main caveat raised was that higher mortgage rates could weigh on real estate activity and thus Digital Real Estate Services growth in FY2027.

bull_case: Foxtel divestiture simplified the portfolio around higher-margin, faster-growing digital pillars (Dow Jones, Digital Real Estate, Book Publishing), driving margin expansion (16.7% to 18% in FY2026)
AI content-licensing deals (OpenAI, Meta, Bloomberg) represent a new, largely incremental high-margin revenue stream monetizing decades of proprietary archives
REA Group and Move/realtor.com give News Corp leveraged exposure to a long-term digital real estate marketplace opportunity with strong network effects and pricing power
Dow Jones' $1B EBITDA five-year target implies a credible, management-articulated growth roadmap for the largest profit segment
Strong Wall Street sentiment with a consensus Strong Buy rating and average price targets implying meaningful upside versus the current price
bear_case: News Media segment faces structural secular decline in print advertising and circulation that could persist indefinitely
AI search/chatbot disintermediation threatens to erode referral traffic and subscription funnels even as the company separately monetizes AI licensing
Real estate segment growth is exposed to housing market cyclicality and higher mortgage rates, a headwind management has explicitly flagged for FY2027
Dual-class share structure concentrates control with the Murdoch family, limiting corporate governance influence for outside shareholders and raising succession-related uncertainty
Ongoing antitrust/ad-tech litigation and regulatory subpoenas involving Google create legal cost and uncertainty around future content-licensing economics
